relevant_group_routes.relationship: Race in the history of white women and gender in the Canadian West: the 'scarcity model' and 'volcano theory' of gender imbalance traced to colonial promoters (1995), and white masculinity, mixed-race relationships and assisted female migration in colonial British Columbia read as the making of whiteness (2001)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. '“Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men”', BC Studies 105/106 (1995), pp. 27–44, read at pp. 27–33 and 42–43: Canadian historians used 'the "scarcity model" (the notion that women's experience improves commensurately with their scarcity) and the "volcano theory" of male sexuality (the assumption of a fixed quantity of male sexual energy)' (p. 27); 'a quarter-century of inquiry into women's history has produced little on the effect of a skewed demography on women's experience' (p. 28); its 'most clear example' is Jan Noel's 'New France: Les femmes favorisées' (p. 29 n. 4); both models 'are based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race. Practitioners of the "scarcity model" never compute aboriginal women (or, for that matter, men) into their arithmetical evaluation' (p. 30); they are 'integral not only to twentieth century scholarship, but also to colonial discourse itself' (p. 31), descending from Wakefield and the colonial promoters (p. 32); white women's experience 'was never determined by gender alone. British Columbia was a class society' (p. 42); 'While gender imbalance increased white women's opportunities for heterosexual contact, it restricted those economic and social possibilities not contained within the heterosexual nexus' (p. 43). On the Edge of Empire (2001) is unread; Orlowski (p. 119) quotes its aim, 'the importance of race to the social experience of gender in nineteenth-century British Columbia' (p. 8), and 'a sharp disjuncture between colonial discourse and colonial practice on this edge of empire' (p. 167, quoted p. 120; Carter, p. 119, uses the same phrase). In-period reception, read in full: Carter (2002): 'This book also makes a valuable Canadian contribution to "Whiteness" studies' (p. 117); Rutherdale (2002): 'At the heart of this imagined community was Whiteness' (p. 325), and the reformers' hope that white women were the 'imperial panacea' (p. 4, as quoted p. 326). Critics: Orlowski (2002) holds that she 'fails to invoke what Roediger calls the "wages of whiteness"', leaving 'a binary racial divide that runs through the entire book but did not run through colonial British Columbia', with Chinese labourers set aside (p. 121), and that her claim that 'class relations are central to social relations' receives little attention (p. 121); Carter (p. 119) asks for the North American setting ('This edge of empire had much in common with California'); Rutherdale's 'small quibble' is that the 'Home' and 'Away' relationship 'could be further probed' (p. 326). Distinct from the Van Kirk packet's edges on fur-trade women: this edge is the post-fur-trade settler colony and the critique of the scarcity model.
